steps.body: The ten-frame gives EVERY amount a shape: a full row is five at a glance, so seven reads as five-and-two with no counting.
steps.narration: The ten-frame gives EVERY amount a shape: a full row is five at a glance, so seven reads as five-and-two with no counting.

widget.prompt: Build 7 on the frame — fill the top row, then two below.

commonCounts.feedback: That is the full row alone; two more dots complete the seven.
That adds one too many below; five and two make seven.

widget.missFeedback: Fill the whole top row first, then add the extras beneath.
widget.successFeedback: Seven, read as five-and-two — the full row does the counting for you.

predict.prompt: On a ten-frame, a full row plus two more reads as…
predict.reveal: The full row is a known five; only the extras need noticing.

cml.actionGoal: Pair each object with exactly one number and trust the last number said for kch subitize frame.
invariants: A count pairs objects with number words one to one, and its last word names the whole group — which is why order, spacing, and arrangement can change without changing the answer for kch subitize frame.
misconceptions: Skipping or double-counting an object, recounting when nothing changed, or believing a spread-out group holds more.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If one more object joined the group, what would the last counting word become?

widget.prompt: Why does a ten-frame make a quick look easier?

options.label: Rows make a known dot pattern
options.feedback: Correct — a full row is five at a glance, so the eye reads “five and some more” instead of counting.

options.label: The frame makes the dots larger
options.feedback: Size does not help naming amounts; the fixed positions do.

options.label: The frame hides the extra dots
options.feedback: Nothing is hidden — every dot sits in its own square, which is what makes them readable.

options.label: Frames only ever hold ten
options.feedback: A frame can hold fewer; its power is showing HOW MANY of the ten squares are filled.

widget.prompt: Look at the ten-frame flash and choose the matching numeral.

commonPicks.feedback: 3 misses 1 of the visible dots. Group the dots, then count the full group as 4.
5 counts 1 extra. Touch each dot once in your mind — the group holds 4.

widget.successFeedback: Yes — 5! You saw it like a dice face.

widget.prompt: Start at 11 and count on 3. Tap where you land.

commonLandings.feedback: 13 stops one complete hop too soon. Continue the final 1-unit hop to reach 14.
15 goes one complete hop too far. Count just 3 hops from 11 to land on 14.

widget.missFeedback: Start at 11 and count on 3: you land on 14.
widget.successFeedback: 11 and 3 more is 14 — counting on continues the count instead of starting over.
widget.lowFeedback: Short of the landing — all 3 counts are needed to reach 14.
widget.highFeedback: Past the landing — the count-on stops after 3 numbers, on 14.
